passages.t: Woe to the destroyer, and a prayer for grace
passages.happening:
“Woe to you, O destroyer never destroyed, O traitor never betrayed!” (verse 1). When the destroyer has finished destroying, he will be destroyed; when he has finished betraying, he will be betrayed.

Then a prayer: “O LORD, be gracious to us! We wait for You.” (verse 2). ‘Be our strength every morning and our salvation in time of trouble’ (verse 2). The peoples flee at the thunder of his voice (verse 3), and their spoil is stripped as if by locusts (verse 4).

‘The LORD is exalted, for He dwells on high; He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness’ (verse 5). ‘He will be the sure foundation for your times, a storehouse of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The fear of the LORD is Zion’s treasure’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 33 closes the series of woes that began in chapter 28. Five were aimed at Israel and Judah. This last one is aimed at the enemy, the destroyer who has not yet been destroyed.

The destroyer is not named, but most interpreters identify him with Assyria and Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC. The chapter's mix of prayer, oracle and hymn has led some interpreters to take it as a liturgy used in worship during or after the crisis.

The prayer of verse 2 asks for strength every morning, the daily strength of people under siege. And verse 6 names what Zion's real wealth is: not silver or alliances, but the fear of the LORD.
passages.later: A psalm asks for the same daily mercy: ‘Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning’ (Psalm 30:5). And Isaiah had seen the same destroyer in an earlier vision: ‘The traitor still betrays, and the destroyer still destroys’ (Isaiah 21:2).
passages.asks: Zion's treasure is the fear of the LORD. Ask what you treat as your treasure. And ask whether you pray for strength one morning at a time, as these people did.

passages.t: Who can dwell with the consuming fire?
passages.happening:
‘Behold, their valiant ones cry aloud in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly’ (verse 7). The highways are deserted. ‘The treaty has been broken, the witnesses are despised, and human life is disregarded’ (verse 8). The land mourns. Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel wither (verse 9).

The LORD says he will now arise and be exalted (verse 10). The enemies conceive chaff and give birth to stubble; their own breath will consume them (verse 11). Far and near will hear what he has done (verses 12-13).

‘The sinners in Zion are afraid’ (verse 14). They ask who can dwell with the consuming fire. The answer: ‘He who walks righteously and speaks with sincerity, who refuses gain from extortion, whose hand never takes a bribe’ (verse 15), who stops his ears from plots of murder and shuts his eyes to evil. ‘He will dwell on the heights; the mountain fortress will be his refuge; his food will be provided and his water assured’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The broken treaty of verse 8 fits the account in 2 Kings 18: Hezekiah admitted his rebellion and paid Sennacherib a heavy tribute of silver and gold, and yet the Assyrian king still sent his officials and an army against Jerusalem. The weeping envoys of peace may be Hezekiah's negotiators coming back with nothing.

Lebanon with its forests, the Plain of Sharon on the coast, Bashan east of the Sea of Galilee with its oaks, and Mount Carmel were the most fertile regions of the land. When they wither, the whole land mourns.

Then the question turns inward. The sinners in Zion realize that the God who burns up the enemy is a fire they too must face. The answer, in the form of the old temple entrance psalms, is a life of honesty and justice: no extortion, no bribes, no part in violence. The first hearers were told that safety in God's presence belongs to the righteous, not merely to those who live in Jerusalem.
passages.later: The psalms ask the same question at the temple gate: ‘O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?’ (Psalm 15:1), and answer, ‘He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness’ (Psalm 15:2). Hebrews says, ‘For our God is a consuming fire’ (Hebrews 12:29).
passages.asks: The sinners in Zion asked who could live with the consuming fire. Ask whether you think of God's holiness as a danger only to others. And ask which part of verse 15 your life most needs: honest speech, clean hands, or eyes shut to evil.

passages.t: The King in his beauty, and a tent that will not move
passages.happening:
‘Your eyes will see the King in His beauty and behold a land that stretches afar’ (verse 17). They will think back on the old terror: where is the one who counted the tribute and the towers (verse 18)? They will no longer see the insolent people of a foreign speech they could not understand (verse 19).

‘Look upon Zion, the city of our appointed feasts’ (verse 20). Jerusalem will be a peaceful pasture, a tent whose pegs will never be pulled up. There the Majestic One will be like a place of wide rivers, where no warship can row (verse 21). ‘For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us’ (verse 22).

The enemy's rigging hangs slack and useless; even the lame will carry off plunder (verse 23). And no one living in Zion will say they are sick; ‘The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The officials of verse 18 who tallied, weighed and counted the towers are the officers of an occupying power who counted tribute and surveyed the city's defenses. They will be only a bad memory.

Jerusalem had no great river, unlike Babylon or Egypt with their waterways full of ships. Here God himself is the city's river, broad and safe, where no enemy fleet can sail. A tent whose pegs are never pulled up is a picture of permanence for people who remembered their tent-dwelling ancestors.

The chapter ends with the King seen in his beauty, the LORD as judge, lawgiver and king, and a people healed and forgiven together. Healing and forgiveness belong together in God's promised future. That is a promise about his kingdom, not a statement that anyone's illness now comes from their sin.
passages.later: A psalm sings, ‘There is a river whose streams delight the city of God’ (Psalm 46:4). And Revelation promises a city where ‘there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain’ (Revelation 21:4).
passages.hard:
Does verse 24 mean that sickness comes from sin, so that forgiveness brings healing?

The verse sets healing and forgiveness side by side in the picture of God's future city. In that city, no one will say they are sick, and everyone will be forgiven. It is a promise of a world made whole, body and soul together.

It does not teach that a person who is ill today is ill because of some sin, or that a sick believer has not been forgiven. Elsewhere Scripture firmly rejects that reasoning, as in the book of Job and in Jesus' answer about the man born blind.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people will see the King in his beauty, and the tent of Zion will never be moved. Ask what you long to see when the old terrors are only memories. And ask whether you can live now as a citizen of the city whose King is also its judge and lawgiver.
